explanations.explanation: Prayed is it. The LORD says He is speaking because “you have prayed to Me” about Sennacherib king of Assyria (Isaiah 37:21). Hezekiah's prayer is written out in Isaiah 37:15-20. Isaiah carries the message, and it starts with the praying, not with the army.

No offering is mentioned in this verse. The LORD says He is speaking because “you have prayed to Me” (Isaiah 37:21). You can read what Hezekiah prayed in Isaiah 37:15-20. This message names words spoken to the LORD.

Singing is a fine thing, friend, and I hum at my ovens all day long. But it's not what this verse says. The LORD speaks because “you have prayed to Me” (Isaiah 37:21), and Hezekiah's prayer is written in Isaiah 37:15-20.

Despises, that's the word. “The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you,” the LORD says (Isaiah 37:22). That's Zion pictured as a daughter. I bet that's not the welcome a king with that much bragging was hoping for.

Fear is a fair guess with an Assyrian king in the picture, but it's not what the LORD says. Verse 22 says Zion “despises you and mocks you.” That's Zion pictured as a daughter, and she isn't cowering in this line.

Obeying isn't in this verse at all. The words are “despises you and mocks you” (Isaiah 37:22). Nobody in this line is taking orders from Sennacherib, friend. Zion is pictured as a daughter, and she's doing the mocking.

The Holy One of Israel, and the LORD asks it as a question first: “Whom have you taunted and blasphemed?” The answer comes with an exclamation point: “Against the Holy One of Israel!” (Isaiah 37:23). Sennacherib sent his taunts through his servants (Isaiah 37:24). Verse 23 says who they were really aimed at.

The king of Babylon isn't the one in this question. The LORD asks, “Whom have you taunted and blasphemed?” and answers, “Against the Holy One of Israel!” (Isaiah 37:23). Sennacherib's taunts went out through his servants (Isaiah 37:24), but verse 23 names who they were aimed at.

Moab's king isn't named anywhere in these verses. The LORD asks, “Whom have you taunted and blasphemed?” and then answers it Himself: “Against the Holy One of Israel!” (Isaiah 37:23). The taunts were sent through Sennacherib's servants (Isaiah 37:24). That's who was on the receiving end.

True. Sennacherib says it himself: “I have cut down its tallest cedars, the finest of its cypresses” (Isaiah 37:24). That comes right after the chariots and the remote peaks of Lebanon, and he's still going. The man brags like he's reading his list of achievements at a company awards night.

That one is actually in there. Sennacherib says, “I have cut down its tallest cedars, the finest of its cypresses” (Isaiah 37:24). The LORD is repeating his own words back to him. It does sound like a lot of lumber for one boast, friend.

He planned it long ago. The LORD says, “Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it” (Isaiah 37:26). So when Sennacherib talks like it was all his doing, he sounds like the coworker who stands up in the meeting and takes credit for the whole project. The verse goes on, “Now I have brought it to pass, that you should crush fortified cities into piles of rubble.”

Chance is my excuse every time a batch burns, friend, but it's not what verse 26 says. The LORD says, “Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it.” Then He adds, “Now I have brought it to pass…” (Isaiah 37:26).
No Assyrian god is named in verse 26. The LORD says, “Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it” (Isaiah 37:26). So the plan belongs to the LORD. He also says He has now brought it to pass.

That's the opposite of the picture. The LORD says the people are “devoid of power,” and then compares them to “tender green shoots, grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown” (Isaiah 37:27). Mighty trees don't get scorched before they're grown. I think it's a sad picture, friend.

False. The people are “devoid of power,” “dismayed and ashamed,” and the LORD says, “They are like plants in the field, tender green shoots, grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown” (Isaiah 37:27). Mighty trees would be the opposite picture. I think it's a sad one.

Not unnoticed at all. The LORD says, “But I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me” (Isaiah 37:28). Verse 29 adds that his “rage and arrogance against Me have reached My ears.” None of it slipped past.

False. The LORD says, “But I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me” (Isaiah 37:28). Then verse 29 says his “rage and arrogance against Me have reached My ears.” Sitting, going out, coming in, raging: the LORD knows all of it.

explanations.answer: Send him back the way he came
explanations.explanation: Back the way he came. After the hook and the bit, the verse says, “send you back the way you came” (Isaiah 37:29). Same road, opposite direction. Anybody who's ever missed an exit on the highway knows that trip.

explanations.answer: Lead him into Jerusalem in chains
explanations.explanation: Chains and Jerusalem aren't in this verse. The LORD says He will “send you back the way you came” (Isaiah 37:29). So Sennacherib is headed back, not in. The verse gives the direction, and it points away.

explanations.answer: Hand him over to the king of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Verse 29 doesn't hand him to anyone. Egypt only shows up earlier, in his boast about drying up its streams (Isaiah 37:25). What the LORD says here is “send you back the way you came.” That's the whole plan in this verse.

explanations.answer: They will sow and reap again
explanations.explanation: They will sow and reap again. The sign says, “in the third year you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit” (Isaiah 37:30). Two years of the land growing things on its own, then the work boots go back on. Vineyards are part of that third-year picture too.

explanations.answer: They will leave the land for good
explanations.explanation: Leaving isn't in this sign. The third year says, “you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit” (Isaiah 37:30). Verse 31 says the remnant of Judah “will again take root below.” That sounds like roots going down, not bags being packed.

explanations.answer: They will live off the king's storehouses
explanations.explanation: Storehouses aren't mentioned in this sign. The first two years are about what grows on its own. The third year says, “you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit” (Isaiah 37:30). So the food comes from the ground, not from the king's storehouses.

True. Verse 31 says, “the surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above.” A remnant is the ones who are left, and here the text says they will take root again. Roots down, fruit up: that's a plant with its priorities in order.

That one is in there. Verse 31 says, “the surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above.” The survivors are pictured like a plant that grows again. Roots go down, fruit goes up, friend.

explanations.answer: The zeal of the LORD of Hosts
explanations.explanation: The zeal of the LORD of Hosts. Verse 32 says it plainly: “The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.” The remnant and the survivors go forth from Jerusalem and Mount Zion, and the credit goes to the LORD. There's no army in that sentence.

Hezekiah's army isn't named in verse 32. The verse says, “The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.” There's no army in that sentence, friend, not even a cookie-sized one. The remnant goes forth from Jerusalem, and the credit goes to the LORD.

explanations.answer: The help of the king of Cush
explanations.explanation: Tirhakah, king of Cush, comes up earlier in this chapter (Isaiah 37:9). But verse 32 gives the credit somewhere else: “The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.” No outside help is named in that sentence. The remnant and the survivors go forth because of the LORD's zeal.

That's flipped. Verse 33 says the king of Assyria will not “build up a siege ramp against it.” The same verse says he “will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it.” Everything on his list comes back as a no.

False. The LORD says Sennacherib “will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it,” and that he will not “build up a siege ramp against it” (Isaiah 37:33). The whole list is a no: no entering, no arrow, no shield, no ramp.

explanations.answer: For His own sake and David's
explanations.explanation: For His own sake and David's. The LORD says He will defend the city and save it “for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David” (Isaiah 37:35). He names two sakes, and only two. That's all the reason the verse gives.

Hezekiah and Isaiah matter in this story, since Hezekiah prayed and Isaiah carried the message (Isaiah 37:21). But verse 35 names different sakes. The LORD says, “for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.” His own and David's are the pair.

explanations.answer: For the priests' sake and the people's
explanations.explanation: Priests and people aren't named in verse 35. The LORD says He will save the city “for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.” That's two sakes, and neither one is on your list. The verse stops at those two.

Nineveh. Verse 37 says, “He returned to Nineveh and stayed there.” Back in verse 34 the LORD said the king would go back the way he came, and here he is heading home. Broke camp, withdrew, Nineveh: that's the whole trip in one verse.

Babylon isn't where he heads. Verse 37 says, “He returned to Nineveh and stayed there.” He breaks camp and withdraws, and Nineveh is the place the text gives. Babylon isn't named in these verses at all.
Damascus isn't named in this passage. Verse 37 says, “He returned to Nineveh and stayed there.” After the angel strikes the camp, he breaks camp and withdraws. Nineveh is where the text sends him.

Ararat. After they put him to the sword, Adrammelech and Sharezer “escaped to the land of Ararat” (Isaiah 38:38 is not it; it's Isaiah 37:38). The text gives their names and the place they went. Then it turns to who takes the throne.

Egypt shows up earlier in the chapter, in Sennacherib's bragging about its streams (Isaiah 37:25). It isn't where the sons head, though. Verse 38 says they “escaped to the land of Ararat.” That's the destination the text gives.
Babylon isn't named in this passage. Verse 38 says the sons “escaped to the land of Ararat.” That's the one place the text gives them. Their names, Adrammelech and Sharezer, come right before it.
Esar-haddon. Verse 38 says, “And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place.” Three sons are named in that verse, and one takes the throne. It isn't either of the two who escaped.

Shalmaneser was an Assyrian king in the Bible (2 Kings 17:3), but verse 38 doesn't name him here. It says, “And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place.” One name in the verse takes the throne, and it's that one.

Tiglath-pileser was an Assyrian king in the Bible too (2 Kings 15:29), but he isn't in this verse. Verse 38 says, “And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place.” The text names one king taking over, and it's Sennacherib's son.
